finding.blocking_rationale: REQ-2 requires that no price history entry is lost except by an explicit delete. This loses it on the documented ingestion path, inside the operating envelope (one writer, the README's first example), and the loss cannot be undone once the launch has run.
finding.description: ListingStore.upsert_listing writes a listing that already exists with INSERT OR REPLACE INTO listings. For an existing row, REPLACE resolves the conflict by deleting the existing row and inserting a new one. open_store sets PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON and migration 2 declares price_history.listing_id REFERENCES listings (id) ON DELETE CASCADE, so SQLite runs the cascade for that delete and removes every price_history row of the listing. The code then appends a history row only if the price changed: after a re-scrape with a changed price the history is just the new price, and after a re-scrape with an unchanged price, the common case, it is empty. No error, no warning. The method carries the previous id and first_seen_at into the REPLACE, so the id stays stable, which is what the existing tests check.
finding.evidence: Reproduction through the public API, on a new store: upsert_listing('kleinanzeigen', '1', price='100 €', currency='EUR', ...) at t0, then the same listing with price='90 €' at t0 + 1 h: price_history returns only the 9000 entry, the 10000 entry is gone. A third upsert with price='90 €' at t0 + 2 h: price_history returns [].
finding.impact: Every re-scrape of a known listing, the most frequent operation of the system, silently and irreversibly destroys its price history, which the search agents use to spot price drops.
finding.title: Every re-scrape deletes the listing's price history
finding.verification: After a first upsert, re-scrapes with changed and unchanged prices and a watcher update, price_history returns the first price followed by every later change, get_listing keeps the original id and first_seen_at, and delete_listing still removes the listing together with its history.

finding.blocking_rationale: REQ-1 requires the exact number of minor units on all three paths, with '19,99 €' as its criterion's own example. The formats and amounts that fail are inside the operating envelope, and the buyers enrolled in the validation would see wrong prices.
finding.description: parse_amount returns the amount as a binary float (float(price) for numbers, float of the whole and fraction for text). Each ingestion path converts it with its own copy of int(amount * factor): upsert_listing in store.py, apply_update in updates.py and import_records in bulk.py. float('19.99') is 19.98999999999999843..., times 100 is 1998.9999999999998, and int() truncates it to 1998. About 4.6% of the amounts from 0.00 to 999.99 come out one minor unit short, always down, common retail prices among them: 19.99, 69.99, 17.99, 4.35, 8.20.
finding.evidence: upsert_listing('kleinanzeigen', '1', title='x', price='19,99 €', currency='EUR', ...) followed by get_listing(...)['price_minor'] gives 1998, not 1999. The same amounts come out short through apply_update and import_records.
finding.impact: Buyers are sent prices one minor unit below what the marketplace shows (19.98 € for an item priced 19.99 €), and a real change of one minor unit can vanish from the history.
finding.title: Prices are stored one minor unit short on all three ingestion paths
finding.verification: '19,99 €', 19.99, '£17.99', '4,35 €' and '8.20' stored through upsert_listing, apply_update and import_records give price_minor 1999, 1999, 1799, 435 and 820, and amounts that land just above the integer in floating point ('1,10 €', '2.20', 0.55) are still exact.

fix.summary: upsert_listing updates a known listing in place with UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? and inserts a new one with INSERT, so no row is deleted and the cascade never runs.
parse_amount returns an exact Decimal, reading a float price by its shortest decimal representation, so int(amount * factor) at the three call sites is exact.

data.evidence: Re-ran the finding's reproduction on the fixed candidate: after upserts at 100 €, 90 € and 90 € again the history is 100.00, 90.00; a watcher update to 85 € appends 85.00; get_listing keeps the original id and first_seen_at; delete_listing still removes the listing and its history. The fixture suite passes.
data.scope_evidence: One commit; in listings/store.py it changes only upsert_listing's write, which is what the finding needs.

data.evidence: '19,99 €', 19.99, '£17.99', '4,35 €' and '8.20' are stored as 1999, 1999, 1799, 435 and 820 through upsert_listing, apply_update and import_records; '1,10 €', '2.20' and 0.55 remain exact.
data.scope_evidence: One commit; in listings/prices.py it changes only parse_amount's return type, the root cause, and no call site.

data.justification: Commit eca23b1 ('refactor(store): write new and known listings with one statement') replaced the UPDATE/INSERT split that had resolved F-0001 with a single INSERT OR REPLACE that passes the previous row's id. SQLite implements REPLACE as DELETE + INSERT; with foreign_keys = ON and price_history ON DELETE CASCADE, the delete cascades and removes all price_history rows. Reproduction on this candidate confirms the history is empty after a re-scrape with unchanged price, and contains only the latest price after a re-scrape with changed price. The verifier's confirmation on e59b1a1 is no longer valid for this candidate because the code it verified has been replaced.

finding.blocking_rationale: REQ-2 requires that no price history entry is lost except by an explicit delete. This loses it on the documented ingestion path, inside the envelope, on every re-scrape. The bounded launch would accumulate 14 days of scrapes that silently erase the very data the validation is meant to evaluate. Resolving it after the launch would mean discarding the collected data and re-running.
finding.description: Commit eca23b1 replaced the UPDATE/INSERT split in ListingStore.upsert_listing with a single INSERT OR REPLACE INTO listings that passes the previous row's id when the listing is known. SQLite implements REPLACE as: delete the conflicting row, then insert the new one. open_store sets PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, and migration 2 declares price_history.listing_id REFERENCES listings(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. The delete therefore cascades and removes every price_history row of the listing before the new row is inserted. The code then appends a history row only when the price changed, so after a re-scrape with an unchanged price (the common case) the history is empty, and after a re-scrape with a changed price the history is just the new price. The previous fix for F-0001 (UPDATE for known listings, INSERT for new ones) is undone.
finding.evidence:
Reproduction on this candidate (commit eca23b1), fresh database:

  from listings import open_store
  from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta
  t0 = datetime(2026,1,1,tzinfo=timezone.utc)
  with open_store('t.db') as s:
      s.upsert_listing('kleinanzeigen','1', title='x', price='100 €', currency='EUR', url='u', category='bikes', seen_at=t0)
      s.upsert_listing('kleinanzeigen','1', title='x', price='90 €', currency='EUR', url='u', category='bikes', seen_at=t0+timedelta(hours=1))
      s.upsert_listing('kleinanzeigen','1', title='x', price='90 €', currency='EUR', url='u', category='bikes', seen_at=t0+timedelta(hours=2))
      print(s.price_history('kleinanzeigen','1'))  # []

Expected after the three calls: [{10000, t0}, {9000, t0+1h}]. Got: [].

Also: 100€ -> 90€ -> 80€ yields history [{8000, t0+2h}] only, losing both 10000 and 9000.

The existing test suite does not catch this: test_rescrape_with_a_new_price_sets_the_current_price only asserts get_listing()['price_minor'], not price_history.
finding.impact: Every re-scrape of a known listing (the most frequent operation) silently and irreversibly destroys its price history. Inside the envelope (one ingestion process, 17 backends, up to 50,000 listings over 14 days), buyers in the validation will see listings with no price-drop signal, which is the feature the search agents are meant to provide. The loss is irreversible once the launch has run.
finding.title: upsert_listing uses INSERT OR REPLACE, which cascades and deletes the listing's price history on every re-scrape
finding.verification: After a first upsert at 100€, a re-scrape at 90€ and a third re-scrape at 90€ again, price_history returns [{10000, t0}, {9000, t0+1h}]; a further re-scrape at 80€ appends {8000, t0+2h}; get_listing keeps the original id and first_seen_at; delete_listing still removes the listing and its history; apply_update and import_records paths still append history correctly.
